item.title: TELEPUZ MaaS Emerges as StepSecurity Expands GitHub Actions and VS Code Controls
TuxBot, Gemini CLI Abuse, OpenClaw Flaws, and Zoom CVE-2026-53412
SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days, AsyncAPI npm Compromise, and ClaudeFix MacSync Stealer
Microsoft 622-CVE Patch Tuesday: Exploited SharePoint, ADFS Flaws and Critical Browser Updates
CISA Warns on Exploited SharePoint CVEs as AsyncAPI npm and DriveSurge Campaigns Spread Malware
CVE-2026-56164 SharePoint, SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-days, AsyncAPI npm compromise, ClickFix malware
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-15409, CVE-2026-15410: SonicWall SMA 1000 zero-day vulnerabilities exploited in the wild — Must Read

SonicWall patched two SMA 1000 zero-day vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, that have been exploited in the wild and may be chained for unauthenticated remote code execution. Organizations should urgently update affected appliances and review SonicWall’s indicators of compromise.

  • SonicWall patched CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410 in its SMA 1000 Series secure remote access appliances after confirming exploitation in the wild.
  • CVE-2026-15409 is a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the SMA 1000 Workplace interface with a CVSSv3 score of 10.
  • CVE-2026-15410 is a code injection vulnerability in the Appliance Management Console that can allow remote code execution and has a CVSSv3 score of 7.2.
  • The article states that the two vulnerabilities may be chained to create a fully remote, unauthenticated path to arbitrary operating system command execution on affected appliances.
  • SonicWall released fixed versions for SMA1000 models 6210, 7210, and 8200v, and CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog with a remediation date of July 17.

CISA warns admins to patch actively exploited SharePoint flaws — Must Read

CISA is warning admins to urgently patch on-premises Microsoft SharePoint servers because attackers are actively exploiting three flaws to bypass authentication, execute code, steal IIS machine keys, and maintain persistence. Federal agencies must secure systems affected by the latest exploited flaw by July 17 or take them offline if they cannot be mitigated.

  • CISA warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, and CVE-2026-56164 to hack Internet-exposed on-premises SharePoint Server instances.
  • The three actively exploited flaws affect all supported self-hosted SharePoint Server versions, including SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.
  • CISA said attackers are using the flaws to bypass authentication, gain remote code execution, steal Internet Information Services machine keys, gain persistence, and deploy malware on compromised systems.
  • Shadowserver currently tracks nearly 10,000 Internet-exposed Microsoft SharePoint servers, including more than 800 that are unpatched against CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659.
  • CISA recommended applying Microsoft’s latest patches, verifying successful installation, shortening patching cycles, enabling AMSI integration for SharePoint web applications, using Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections, and reducing direct Internet exposure.

AsyncAPI npm packages infected with credential-stealing malware — Must Read

Attackers compromised AsyncAPI GitHub Actions workflows to publish five malicious npm package versions that installed credential-stealing remote access malware while still appearing to come from legitimate trusted releases. The packages have been removed, but anyone who installed them during the July 14 exposure window should remove payloads, regenerate lock files, and rotate credentials.

  • Five malicious versions of AsyncAPI packages were published to npm in a supply-chain attack that delivered a remote access trojan with information-stealing capabilities.
  • The attacker exploited a misconfigured GitHub Actions workflow, compromised two AsyncAPI GitHub repositories on July 14, and used the legitimate release workflow with npm’s GitHub OIDC trusted-publisher integration to publish the packages.
  • The malicious packages were @asyncapi/generator 3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers 1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components 0.7.1, and @asyncapi/specs 6.11.2-alpha.1 and 6.11.2.
  • The final payload establishes persistence, communicates with command-and-control servers over HTTP, Nostr relays, Ethereum smart contracts, and a libp2p mesh network, and appears intended to steal credentials, tokens, browser data, CI/CD secrets, AI developer tool data, cryptocurrency wallets, and database information.
  • All five malicious package versions have been removed from npm, but existing installations and lock files created during the July 14 exposure window may still contain the malicious releases.

Microsoft smashes Patch Tuesday record for second successive month — Must Read

Microsoft’s July Patch Tuesday fixed a record 622 vulnerabilities, including two already exploited flaws in SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services. The surge underscores rapidly growing vulnerability volumes, likely aided by AI-assisted discovery, while defenders face harder triage due to Microsoft’s less detailed update guide.

  • Microsoft released fixes for more than 600 security vulnerabilities in July, making it the largest Patch Tuesday in the program's history and more than triple the previous record set last month.
  • Microsoft's Security Update Guide no longer lists the individual CVEs in the Patch Tuesday batch, instead showing a summary table by product family and a “Notable CVEs” section, while individual advisories remain available separately.
  • Microsoft said two flaws patched this month are being exploited in the wild: CVE-2026-56164 in on-premises SharePoint Server and CVE-2026-56155 in Active Directory Federation Services.
  • Rapid7 said CVE-2026-55040 is the first half of an exploit chain that leads to unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable SharePoint server, with the second vulnerability expected to be patched in August.
  • The article says Microsoft and analysts have linked rising vulnerability volumes to AI-assisted tools, while Jerry Gamblin noted that exploited vulnerabilities have not risen at the same pace as published CVEs.

Researcher Drops New Windows Zero-Day PoC Hours After Microsoft Patch Tuesday — Must Read

A researcher released a stripped-down PoC for LegacyHive, a Windows User Profile Service privilege-escalation zero-day that still works on fully patched supported Windows systems after July 2026 Patch Tuesday. The disclosure adds pressure on Microsoft amid active exploitation of newly patched SharePoint Server and ADFS flaws.

  • Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as Nightmare-Eclipse, released a proof-of-concept exploit called LegacyHive for a Windows User Profile Service arbitrary hive load elevation of privileges vulnerability.
  • The LegacyHive proof-of-concept requires another standard user credential and a third username, and if successful it mounts the target user hive in the current user classes root.
  • Chaotic Eclipse said the released exploit was stripped down to prevent public exploitation, while the original exploit did not require additional user credentials and was not limited to the usrclass.dat hive.
  • The article states that LegacyHive works on all supported desktop and server versions of Windows, including systems running the latest July 2026 Patch Tuesday update.
  • Microsoft’s July 2026 Patch Tuesday addressed a record 622 flaws, including actively exploited privilege escalation vulnerabilities in SharePoint Server and Active Directory Federation Services that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

UK Cybercrime Journal: University of Nottingham Breached by ShinyHunters — Must Read

ShinyHunters breached the University of Nottingham and leaked more than 40GB of sensitive student, finance, and personal data, including over 455,000 unique email addresses. The incident appears tied to a wider campaign exploiting a critical Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, with education institutions heavily targeted.

  • On 9 June 2026, the University of Nottingham was listed as a victim on the ShinyHunters Tor data leak site.
  • ShinyHunters leaked over 40GB of billing and payment records, student finance data, and campus portal exports from the University of Nottingham and its Malaysia and China campuses.
  • Have I Been Pwned analysis found the leaked data contained over 455,000 unique email addresses along with personal information including ethnicities, disabilities, and passport numbers.
  • Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group attributed an active compromise and extortion campaign targeting Oracle PeopleSoft application infrastructure to UNC6240, also known as ShinyHunters.
  • The campaign used a critical Oracle PeopleSoft remote code execution vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-35273, according to Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group.

Zoom warns of critical account takeover vulnerability — Must Read

Zoom patched a critical Windows flaw, CVE-2026-53412, that could let unauthenticated attackers take over accounts via network access. Users should update Zoom Workplace, VDI Client, and Meeting SDK for Windows immediately.

  • Zoom warned of a critical improper input validation vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-53412, in its desktop client and software development kit for Windows.
  • CVE-2026-53412 has a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and may allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an account takeover via network access.
  • The flaw affects Zoom Workplace for Windows before version 7.0.0, the Windows VDI Client before versions 7.0.10, 6.6.15, and 6.5.18, and the Meeting SDK for Windows before version 7.0.0.
  • Zoom recommends that users apply the latest updates to mitigate the risks from CVE-2026-53412.
  • Zoom’s latest security patches also address three high-severity Windows-related flaws tracked as CVE-2026-53410, CVE-2026-53409, and CVE-2026-53411, and there are no indications at disclosure that any fixed vulnerabilities are being exploited.

Thousands of compromised websites abused by DriveSurge in active ClickFix and FakeUpdates campaigns — Must Read

DriveSurge is abusing thousands of compromised websites to run active ClickFix and FakeUpdates campaigns, tricking visitors into installing malware through fake browser or update prompts. The key takeaway is that legitimate-looking compromised sites are being used at scale to deliver social-engineering malware attacks.

  • Thousands of compromised websites are being abused in active campaigns.
  • DriveSurge is identified as the actor abusing the compromised websites.
  • The campaigns are identified as ClickFix and FakeUpdates campaigns.

TELEPUZ: a modular MaaS malware spreading via CLICKFIX-VIDAR chains — Must Read

Elastic Security Labs identified TELEPUZ, a fast-evolving modular malware likely offered as MaaS, spreading through CLICKFIX-VIDAR chains and using WebSocket C2, persistence, UAC bypass, evasion, credential theft, keylogging, and web-injection modules. Its active development and growing VirusTotal submissions suggest the threat is likely to expand despite currently limited C2 infrastructure.

  • Elastic Security Labs is tracking an emerging threat named TELEPUZ that has been spreading via a CLICKFIX-VIDAR infection chain and has been operating since late April 2026 according to collected infrastructure information.
  • The infection chain begins with a ClickFix social engineering page that prompts the user to copy, paste, and execute a Windows PowerShell command, which downloads a VIDAR Go variant that then retrieves the TELEPUZ stager and main payload.
  • TELEPUZ is a 64-bit Windows DLL written in C that is lightweight, modular, and uses obfuscation techniques including garbage instructions, import hashing, custom RC4 string encryption, and indirect syscalls.
  • The malware installs persistence, performs anti-VM and anti-debugger checks, attempts UAC bypass and SYSTEM privilege escalation, registers itself as a Windows service, and communicates with its C2 over WebSockets.
  • TELEPUZ supports 36 commands and can download additional modules for functions such as keylogging, stealing data, web injection, Chromium cookie extraction, screenshots, file operations, process listing, and process hollowing.

Four New OpenClaw Vulnerabilities: When AI Agents Become the Attacker's Execution Layer — Should Read

Cyera researchers disclosed four OpenClaw vulnerabilities that can let attackers use an AI agent’s own privileges to escape filesystem sandboxes, leak secrets, escalate to owner-level control, and gain persistence. The key takeaway is that agentic AI platforms must be treated as high-privilege execution environments requiring strong isolation, identity enforcement, and runtime controls.

  • Cyera researchers discovered four OpenClaw vulnerabilities affecting filesystem isolation, privilege escalation, and data exposure.
  • CVE-2026-44112 is a critical TOCTOU filesystem write escape that can redirect writes outside the sandbox boundary and allow attackers to overwrite sensitive files, modify configurations, plant malicious scripts, or create persistence mechanisms.
  • CVE-2026-44118 is a high-severity MCP loopback privilege escalation flaw where OpenClaw trusts a client-controlled ownership flag, allowing an authenticated local child process to elevate to owner-level privileges.
  • CVE-2026-44115 can expose sensitive environment variables such as API keys or credentials through variable expansion inside unquoted heredocs despite command allowlist validation.
  • Cyera says Shodan shows more than 65,000 and Zoomeye shows more than 180,000 publicly accessible OpenClaw instances as of May 2026.

OkoBot: new sophisticated malware framework targets cryptocurrency users — Should Read

Kaspersky details OkoBot, an active and evolving malware framework delivered via TookPS that targets cryptocurrency users with SSH-based control, hidden browser extensions, keylogging, screen recording, and wallet seed-phrase phishing. The campaign has hit hundreds of victims across more than 25 countries and uses many coordinated modules to steal crypto-related data and credentials.

  • Kaspersky identified OkoBot as an updated TookPS campaign that uses a malware framework with more than 20 payloads and implants to deliver and orchestrate malicious modules via an SSH tunnel.
  • The initial infection is delivered mainly through ClickFix attacks and GitHub-hosted malware masquerading as legitimate software, including a fake SQL Server Management Studio package that was actually Audacity with a malicious implant embedded in one library.
  • After infection, an automated SSH bot collects system information, harvests cryptocurrency wallet files, browser cookies, profiles, and credentials, and sets up Remote Desktop access through a reverse SSH tunnel.
  • OkoBot includes modules such as a hidden browser extension loader, a plugin dispatcher, SeedHunter for Ledger and Trezor seed phrase theft, MC Keylogger, and OkoSpyware for capturing keystrokes and video of targeted application windows.
  • Kaspersky detected hundreds of OkoBot victims in more than 25 countries, with the largest proportions of attacked end users in Brazil, Vietnam, Canada, Mexico, and Türkiye.

ClaudeFix: Shared Claude Chats Meet ClickFix — Should Read

Zscaler researchers found a MacSync Stealer campaign using Google malvertising to send Mac users searching for Claude to shared Claude chats containing ClickFix paste-and-run commands. The attack abused Anthropic’s legitimate chat-sharing feature to appear trustworthy, then deployed a multi-stage macOS infostealer that stole credentials, files, browser data, and cryptocurrency wallet data.

  • Zscaler Threat Hunting identified recent ClickFix attacks that abused Anthropic’s Claude platform by using shareable Claude chats to host malicious paste-and-run instructions.
  • The campaign used Google paid ads to lure Mac users searching for terms such as “claude download” into shared Claude chats that instructed them to run commands leading to MacSync Stealer.
  • The first-stage command used curl with a Base64-obfuscated URL to download and execute a zsh script, which then launched additional stages of the MacSync Stealer infection chain.
  • MacSync Stealer can steal keychain files, browser data, password manager extension data, Telegram files, selected documents, cloud keys, and cryptocurrency wallet data from macOS systems.
  • Zscaler observed the campaign running from June 12–19, 2026, and noted Russian-language comments in the third-stage AppleScript payload.

TuxBot v3 Evolution Shows Signs of LLM-Assisted IoT Botnet Development — Should Read

Researchers uncovered TuxBot v3 Evolution, an IoT botnet framework that appears to have been partly built with LLM assistance, including leftover AI-generated comments and flawed code. Despite bugs, it shows how AI can help a single developer assemble a more ambitious botnet with encrypted C2, fallback channels, DDoS features, and IoT exploitation capabilities.

  • Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 disclosed a previously unreported IoT botnet framework called TuxBot v3 Evolution that shows signs of being developed with large language model assistance.
  • Unit 42 said the analyzed samples contained leftover AI safety disclaimers and raw LLM chain-of-thought reasoning in comments, while several functions failed to work correctly.
  • TuxBot v3 Evolution includes a C-based bot agent, a Go-based command-and-control server with a DDoS-for-hire panel, a custom exploit virtual machine, Docker-based test infrastructure, and an automated build system.
  • The bot agent is designed to brute-force Telnet access using 1,496 credential pairs and includes exploit code targeting more than 30 IoT device families with known vulnerabilities.
  • Unit 42 said shared infrastructure with Kaitori v3.9 and AISURU tooling places the TuxBot operator within the Keksec ecosystem, which is known for running multiple IoT botnet variants in parallel.

Google Gemini CLI abused as a hacking agent, malware botnet operator — Should Read

A Russian-speaking threat actor used Google’s Gemini CLI as an AI hacking agent to migrate and operate a small botnet controlling systems at a dental clinic, with the tool generating code, deploying infrastructure, troubleshooting issues, and managing infected machines through natural-language prompts.

  • A Russian-speaking threat actor known as “bandcampro” used Google’s open-source Gemini CLI AI tool as a hacking agent and to operate a small-scale botnet.
  • Trend Micro researchers said the threat actor used Gemini CLI to migrate the botnet to a new command-and-control infrastructure, including architecture, coding, VPS deployment, Cloudflare configuration, and debugging in six minutes.
  • The botnet controlled eight systems in a dental clinic, and the threat actor used the AI tool to try to access the OpenDental database.
  • Daily operation logs showed the threat actor managed the botnet through natural-language requests, including asking which machines were online, listing files, and generating infection links.
  • Trend Micro said the botnet was lightweight and unsophisticated, using three plain-text files, an in-memory Python HTTP server, PowerShell agents, and persistence through scheduled tasks, WMI events, and registry modifications.

23andMe reaches $18 million settlement with states for massive breach — Should Read

23andMe agreed to an $18 million settlement with 42 state attorneys general over cybersecurity failures tied to a 2023 breach that exposed data from 6.9 million people, including genetic ancestry information. The deal requires stronger security oversight and preserves customers’ rights to delete personal data and destroy genetic samples.

  • A coalition of 42 state attorneys general reached an $18 million settlement with 23andMe over cybersecurity failings that led to a breach exposing information from 6.9 million people, including genetic ancestry data.
  • The settlement requires new data protection measures from the 23andMe Research Institute, including risk assessments, a special board to oversee data security, and indefinite customer rights to destroy genetic samples and delete personal data.
  • New York Attorney General Letitia James’ office said 23andMe initially denied a breach had occurred and later blamed consumers for account configurations and password use.
  • The attorneys general identified failings including no protections against hacks using stolen credentials, insufficient intrusion prevention, lack of breach logging or monitoring, unaddressed known vulnerabilities, and failure to probe atypical login patterns or test new design features.
  • A Missouri bankruptcy court approved a separate settlement in June awarding millions of breach victims a share of a $47 million fund, and the Wojcicki-led 23andMe Research Institute later paid $305 million for 23andMe’s assets.

Dutch police dismantle global crypto investment scam, arrest alleged mastermind — Should Read

Dutch police dismantled a global fake cryptocurrency investment network that allegedly used dozens of call centers and hundreds of staff to defraud tens of thousands of victims out of more than €100 million a month. The alleged mastermind, described as a well-known hacker with Israeli and Polish citizenship, was arrested and extradited to the Netherlands.

  • Dutch police dismantled an international investment fraud network that allegedly tricked tens of thousands of people into fake cryptocurrency schemes.
  • Authorities said the group had operated since at least 2021, running about two dozen call centers across several countries and employing more than 700 people posing as financial advisers.
  • Police said the operation generated more than €100 million a month by convincing victims to invest in bogus trading platforms after building relationships with them by phone and online.
  • A 46-year-old man with Israeli and Polish citizenship, described by Dutch police as a well-known hacker, was arrested in May at a Polish airport after arriving from Dubai and extradited to the Netherlands.
  • Dutch police estimate that victims in the Netherlands alone lost nearly €25 million, and they believe the organization defrauded tens of thousands of people worldwide.

We built a vulnerability vending machine: AI tokens in, zero-days out — Should Read

Intruder says it built an AI-assisted vulnerability research pipeline that uses code slicing and LLMs to find and exploit real bugs, including a blind SQL injection zero-day in the Creative Mail WordPress plugin affecting sites that also use WooCommerce. The finding highlights that AI can already speed up practical zero-day discovery, so detection and patching processes need to keep pace.

  • Intruder built a pipeline that runs a codebase through Joern, generates relevant code slices, and uses LLMs to triage and attempt exploitation of potential vulnerabilities.
  • The pipeline was tested against the top 200 WordPress plugins, with a focus on unauthenticated WordPress plugin attack surface such as REST routes, template hooks, and nopriv AJAX calls.
  • The first vulnerability produced by the pipeline was CVE-2026-3985, a blind SQL injection in the Creative Mail WordPress plugin that requires WooCommerce to be installed alongside it.
  • Intruder says the exploitation agent produced a working proof of concept that could confirm the issue and extract password hashes from the database.
  • The Creative Mail plugin has been pulled from the WordPress store pending review, and Intruder advises users running Creative Mail with WooCommerce to disable it until a patch is available.

Cursor Flaw Lets Malicious Cloned Repositories Trigger Windows Code Execution — Should Read

Cursor on Windows can execute a malicious git.exe placed in a cloned repository’s root simply when the folder is opened, giving attackers code execution as the user without prompts or clicks. The issue reportedly remains unpatched with no advisory, so users should treat untrusted repos as executable content and open them only in isolated environments.

  • On Windows, Cursor can execute a file named git.exe from a project’s root directory when the repository is opened, without a click, approval dialog, or warning.
  • Mindgard reported the flaw to Cursor on December 15, 2025 and published technical details seven months later, stating that there was still no patch or Cursor advisory.
  • Mindgard’s proof of concept used Windows Calculator renamed to git.exe and committed to a repository root, causing Calculator windows to open automatically when the project was opened in Cursor.
  • The Hacker News found no Cursor security advisory covering the issue as of July 15, and no CVE had been assigned.
  • Cymulate reported that similar Windows executable-search behavior affected GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, and the Codex desktop app, with no fixes shipped for those binary-planting reports as of its June 4 write-up.

US charges alleged operators of Russian bulletproof hosting service — Should Read

U.S. prosecutors charged three Russian nationals accused of running the Media Land and ML.Cloud bulletproof hosting services, which allegedly supported ransomware and cybercrime operations causing more than $62 million in damages. The U.S. is also offering up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates or use of the companies.

  • U.S. federal prosecutors unsealed charges against three Russian nationals accused of providing bulletproof hosting services to ransomware gangs that caused over $62 million in damages worldwide.
  • The indictment says Aleksandr Volosovik owned Media Land, Yulia Pankova owned ML.Cloud and assisted with legal and financial matters, and Kirill Zatolokin collected customer payments.
  • Media Land and ML.Cloud allegedly provided infrastructure in multiple countries outside Russia, including China, Finland, the Netherlands, and the United States.
  • The U.S. Department of State is offering up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates of the actors, their malicious cyber activities, or foreign government-linked use of the companies.
  • The United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, and the European Union have imposed sanctions related to Media Land, ML.Cloud, and the named defendants.

Trump administration unveils AI-supported clearinghouse for cyber vulnerabilities — Should Read

The Trump administration launched Gold Eagle, a Treasury-housed federal clearinghouse that uses AI to help government, industry, and critical infrastructure operators find, validate, prioritize, and patch cyber vulnerabilities faster. Officials said the effort depends on reauthorization of the CISA 2015 Act, which expires in September.

  • The Trump administration announced Gold Eagle, an already operative federal clearinghouse that uses artificial intelligence to help industry, critical infrastructure operators, and government detect, prioritize, and patch cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
  • Gold Eagle is housed in the Treasury Department with support from the Pentagon, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and open-source software providers are also participating.
  • A senior White House official said the clearinghouse is ingesting and validating vulnerabilities and that administrators are creating a system to distribute vulnerabilities to stakeholders without risking leaks.
  • Closed source models including Anthropic’s Mythos will be used in the vulnerability-hunting effort, according to the official.
  • Officials said Gold Eagle is made possible by the CISA 2015 Act and that the effort would be fundamentally challenged if Congress does not reauthorize the law before it expires in September.

New critical infrastructure cybersecurity framework features government, regional council options — Should Read

DHS proposed a new public-private critical infrastructure collaboration framework, ANCHOR, to replace the eliminated CIPAC system as the Trump administration pushes more cyber resilience responsibility to state and local levels. Health-ISAC warned that without strong legal protections, companies may hesitate to share sensitive cyber incident details needed for effective risk mitigation.

  • The Department of Homeland Security proposed a new public-private critical infrastructure collaboration system on Tuesday.
  • The proposed system would replace a framework that President Donald Trump eliminated weeks after returning to office.
  • The Trump administration has said it wants to push more cybersecurity resilience responsibilities to the state and local levels.
  • Errol Weiss of Health-ISAC said ANCHOR needs to address legal exposures that often prevent companies from sharing information about sensitive cyber incidents.
  • Weiss said industry leaders had relied on legal protections in the old CIPAC framework to hold candid discussions about sensitive vulnerabilities.

LAPD sidelines relationship with license-plate reader company Flock Safety — Should Read

The LAPD is pausing its use of Flock Safety license-plate reader cameras and not renewing its contract until data ownership, privacy, security, and sharing safeguards are clarified. The move follows an audit finding wrongful stolen-vehicle flags and growing concerns over ALPR data use in immigration enforcement, abortion investigations, and protest tracking.

  • The Los Angeles Police Department is not renewing its contract with automated license plate reader company Flock Safety amid a dispute over who controls the data Flock collects.
  • An inspector general’s audit pushed the LAPD to stop using Flock technology until enforceable privacy and security rules are added.
  • The audit found that over a two-month period, the LAPD investigated 161 car owners whose vehicles Flock wrongly identified as stolen, according to 404 Media.
  • LAPD Chief Information Officer Dean Gialamas said the department will not use Flock until data, privacy, security, and sharing concerns are resolved through a contractual relationship.
  • Flock called the LAPD’s decision a surprise and said it is confident ongoing discussions can address what it described as misconceptions behind the pause.

It Passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. It Was Still a W-2 Heist. — Should Read

A W-2 payroll phishing attempt passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because it came through a legitimate authenticated ISP mailbox, proving that email authentication verifies the sending domain but not the person behind the display name. Defenders should treat authenticated email as only one signal and require out-of-band verification for bulk PII requests.

  • A payroll inbox received an urgent email requesting the 2025 W-2 PDFs for every employee at every location the same day.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC because it was sent from a compromised or attacker-controlled consumer ISP mailbox through the provider’s legitimate mail servers.
  • The email used a display name carrying a company leader’s identity, while the Reply-To pointed to pointdsk.com, a third domain registered roughly two hours before the message was sent.
  • Microsoft scored the message SCL 9 and placed it in Junk, while IRONSCALES quarantined it outright based on impersonation, behavioral, and spam signals.
  • The article emphasizes that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC validate the sending domain, not the human identity claimed in the display name.

Meta, Microsoft, DOJ, and Others Disrupt Southeast Asia Scam Compounds — Should Read

Meta, Microsoft, the U.S. Department of Justice, and other partners disrupted scam compounds in Southeast Asia linked to large-scale online fraud operations. The action highlights growing coordinated pressure on criminal networks that rely on forced labor and digital platforms to run global scams.

  • The article reports on a disruption of scam compounds in Southeast Asia.
  • Meta, Microsoft, and the U.S. Department of Justice are named as participants in the disruption.
  • The article indicates that additional unnamed parties were also involved in the disruption effort.

Over 1.4 Million Accounts Disrupted in Cybercrime Crackdown — Should Read

An international cybercrime crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million accounts linked to online fraud and other illicit activity, highlighting the scale of coordinated law enforcement action against digital crime networks.

  • The article is about a cybercrime crackdown.
  • The crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million accounts.
  • The article’s title emphasizes the large number of accounts affected by the crackdown.

Microsoft: Some Dell PCs shut down after recent Windows updates — May Read

Microsoft is blocking the latest Windows 11 security update on some Dell PCs after a driver incompatibility caused unexpected shutdowns, poor performance, overheating, and battery drain. The issue stems from a conflict between Intel’s IPF Processor Participant driver and a new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface, with a fix expected soon.

  • Microsoft is blocking the KB5101650 Windows 11 security update on some Dell devices because it can cause shutdowns and performance issues.
  • The issue affects only Dell systems after installing the KB5101650 cumulative update for Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2 devices.
  • Microsoft said affected Dell devices may show a yellow exclamation point in Device Manager next to the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.
  • The root cause is an incompatibility between the Intel driver and the new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface introduced in the June 23, 2026 KB5095093 preview cumulative update.
  • Microsoft is working with Dell on a fix and plans to release a resolution for affected devices in the coming days.

Understanding Claude Tag’s access model in Slack and how to configure it securely — May Read

Claude Tag in Slack uses admin-configured shared access bundles rather than the credentials of the user who tags it, so channel membership effectively determines who can direct the agent within that preset scope. Organizations should treat bundle attachments and Slack channel membership as an access-control boundary, using least-privilege bundles, private channels, approval flows, and Claude Enterprise login/RBAC controls.

  • Claude Tag acts on connected services using shared credentials configured by an administrator for a Slack workspace or private channel, rather than the credentials of the user who tags it.
  • In shared Slack channels, Claude Tag uses a service identity model in which one admin-configured access bundle serves everyone in the channel.
  • Organizations can require users to log in to claude.ai and use role-based access control before they may interact with Claude Tag at all.
  • Tenable Research worked with Anthropic’s security team through coordinated disclosure to review Claude Tag’s access model and admin configuration experience.
  • The article recommends auditing access bundles, reviewing channel membership and bundle scope together, scoping bundles minimally, managing channel invite policies, and using per-user delegation where appropriate.

Harden-Runner Block Mode Now Available for macOS and Windows GitHub-Hosted Runners — May Read

StepSecurity’s Harden-Runner v2.20.0 now supports egress block mode on macOS and Windows GitHub-hosted runners, extending outbound traffic enforcement beyond Linux. This lets teams block unauthorized network calls from compromised workflows or dependencies that could exfiltrate secrets from sensitive build and signing pipelines.

  • Harden-Runner v2.20.0 extends egress block mode to macOS and Windows GitHub-hosted runners.
  • The article says recent GitHub Actions attacks, including Megalodon and GhostAction, relied on outbound calls to exfiltrate secrets.
  • Before this release, Harden-Runner supported egress-policy: block on Linux GitHub-hosted runners, while macOS and Windows GitHub-hosted runners only had audit mode.
  • macOS runners often build and sign iOS and macOS apps using Apple signing certificates, provisioning profiles, and App Store Connect API keys.
  • The recommended path is to start in audit mode, review the recommended policy generated from actual traffic, and then switch to block mode.

Trump’s DNI pick grilled about election security, voter fraud — May Read

Jay Clayton, Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, faced sharp Senate questioning over his refusal to clearly say Joe Biden won the 2020 election and over his views on voter fraud and election security. The hearing raised concerns among Democrats about whether he would preserve intelligence independence and protect election integrity if confirmed.

  • Jay Clayton, President Donald Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, faced questioning from Senate Intelligence Committee Democrats about his independence, election security, and past statements about voter fraud.
  • Clayton repeatedly avoided giving a firm answer that Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, saying instead that Biden became president after U.S. processes were completed.
  • Democrats expressed concern that Clayton could assist Trump’s efforts to undermine the outcomes of past or future elections.
  • Clayton was also questioned about his decision to subpoena journalists reporting on the Air Force One airplane Qatar gifted to Trump.
  • The hearing included little substantive discussion of threats from Russia and China, efforts to shrink the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, or the recent lapse of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act.

There and Back Again: An Operators Guide on NTLM Relaying Egress — May Read

SpecterOps describes a practical NTLM relay technique that coerces SMB or WebDAV authentication out to an internet-facing cloud host, tunnels it back through red team infrastructure, and relays it into the target network to achieve privilege escalation. The key defense is enforcing LDAP signing/LDAPS channel binding, enabling EPA on ADCS web enrollment, and restricting outbound SMB and unnecessary inbound traffic.

  • SpecterOps describes “There and Back Again” as a technique that coerces outbound NTLM authentication to an internet-facing cloud host, forwards it back to red team infrastructure, and proxies it into the target environment to relay to services such as ADCS web enrollment or LDAP/LDAPS.
  • The technique is useful when operators only have low-privilege command-and-control access and cannot bind locally to port 445/TCP or when firewall rules prevent more traditional WebDAV relays inside the environment.
  • The article states that vulnerable ADCS web enrollment endpoints lacking Extended Protection for Authentication are still seen in nearly 70–80% of client environments with an Active Directory presence.
  • The article demonstrates a local privilege escalation flow using WebDAV coercion over port 443/TCP, DNS record creation, EFS and WebClient service preparation, ntlmrelayx relay to LDAPS, shadow credentials, Certipy authentication, S4U2Self, and WMI execution.
  • The defensive guidance recommends enabling LDAP signing and LDAPS channel binding, enabling Extended Protection for Authentication on ADCS web enrollment endpoints, restricting outbound SMB to public IPs, and deploying local firewall rules that allow only necessary inbound ports.

ADPathFinder: OpenGraph Attack Path Mapping in BloodHound CE — Optional

NetSPI released ADPathFinder, an open-source tool that maps and prioritizes Active Directory privilege escalation paths across BloodHound CE data, including AD, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM OpenGraph sources. It also enriches password audit results with BloodHound context so testers can identify cracked credentials that matter most.

  • ADPathFinder maps privilege escalation paths across Active Directory, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM using BloodHound graph data.
  • ADPathFinder combines SharpHound data with OpenGraph collectors such as MSSQLHound and ConfigManBearPig so cross-dataset paths are reported as a single finding instead of separate leads.
  • The tool groups users and computers that reach the same target through the same chain, which can reduce many similar paths in a large graph into one finding with affected principals attached.
  • ADPathFinder can perform password audits from an NTDS dump and hashcat potfile, adding BloodHound context such as group membership, roastability, delegation, and account risk.
  • ADPathFinder writes per-domain HTML reports organized by severity and shared path, with text and JSON outputs available alongside the HTML.

Enrichment Shouldn't Cost You a Lookup: Introducing Censys Unlimited Enrichment — Optional

Censys launched Unlimited Enrichment, a credit-free host enrichment API designed to let security teams enrich every external IP in SIEM, SOAR, and AI SOC workflows without rationing lookups. The key takeaway is that Censys wants IP context to become an always-on first step in alert triage rather than a costly, selective investigation step.

  • Censys introduced Unlimited Enrichment, a credit-free host enrichment API for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
  • Unlimited Enrichment returns a compact, standardized profile that includes geolocation, network and ASN ownership, DNS data, open ports and protocols, labels, Censys ARC Reputation Score, detected threats, and third-party context.
  • Censys designed the API for high-volume automated lookups in SIEM, SOAR, and AI SOC pipelines so teams can enrich alerts at the start of triage instead of rationing lookups.
  • The article describes example uses for firewall, EDR, DLP, and IAM alerts where enrichment data can help analysts decide whether to close, escalate, contain, or investigate further.
  • Unlimited Enrichment is available as an option on the Censys Core plan.

Life Finds a Way: Securing the Enterprise When Everyone Is a Developer — Optional

AI agents and citizen developers are rapidly expanding enterprise attack surfaces and collapsing exploitation timelines, making traditional “do the basics” security programs insufficient. Security teams must adapt to agent-driven scale by securing AI workflows directly and moving as fast as the tools now changing the environment.

  • Gadi Evron argues that AI agents are breaking long-standing security assumptions because configuration, access control, and software creation are becoming less centrally managed and less predictable.
  • The conversation highlights that AI has shortened the time from finding a weakness to exploiting it from weeks to hours, making older patching and response timelines inadequate.
  • Evron says “do the basics” is no longer enough because agents can create new paths, assets, workflows, and exposures that security teams may not know about.
  • Rob Gurzeev says citizen developers and AI-built applications are expanding the attack surface, including AI applications and MCP servers that may expose sensitive company data without proper authentication.
  • Both speakers emphasize that security leaders need to prioritize scale, coverage, and rapid learning because AI tools and risks are changing every few weeks.

Runtime Security for Third-Party GitHub Actions Runners: Bitrise, Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, and Warp — Optional

StepSecurity’s Harden-Runner now supports Bitrise Build Hub macOS runners, extending runtime security for GitHub Actions jobs across Bitrise, Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, and Warp. The key takeaway is that teams using third-party runners can add the same one-step monitoring and egress controls to protect builds from compromised dependencies and actions.

  • StepSecurity’s Harden-Runner v2.20.0 adds support for Bitrise Build Hub macOS runners alongside existing support for Blacksmith, Depot, Namespace, and Warp Build.
  • The article states that moving a GitHub Actions job from GitHub-hosted runners to a third-party runner changes the infrastructure but not the risks, because jobs still check out code, install dependencies, and hold secrets.
  • Harden-Runner can be added as the first step of a GitHub Actions job and provides outbound network monitoring, workflow-step correlation, detections in the StepSecurity dashboard, audit mode, and block mode with allowed endpoints on supported providers.
  • Bitrise support is presented as important for mobile teams because iOS pipelines may contain Apple signing certificates, provisioning profiles, and App Store Connect API keys.
  • The article says Harden-Runner is open source and is used by more than 13,000 open-source projects and enterprises.

Introducing Device Policy: Enforce Approved VS Code Extensions Across Your Fleet — Optional

StepSecurity launched Device Policy to let organizations approve and enforce allowed VS Code extensions across developer machines using native IDE and OS policy mechanisms. Policies can be deployed through MDM tools like Intune, Jamf, and Kandji or enforced directly by the Dev Machine Guard agent.

  • StepSecurity announced Device Policy, which lets organizations define approved VS Code extensions and enforce those decisions on developer machines using the IDE's native policy mechanism.
  • Device Policy builds policies from the extension inventory observed by Dev Machine Guard, allowing teams to approve extensions already used across their fleet.
  • The feature supports version controls such as allowing any version, restricting to stable releases, pinning exact versions, or approving all extensions from a trusted publisher.
  • Profiles can be delivered through existing MDM tools such as Intune, Jamf, or Kandji, or enforced directly by the DMG agent when no MDM is available.
  • Device Policy can also be managed through Terraform using the StepSecurity Terraform provider and a guided one-time import flow.

KAPE 101: A Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor Cheatsheet — Optional

This is a beginner-friendly cheatsheet for using KAPE, Kroll’s forensic artifact collection and processing tool, to quickly gather and parse evidence during incident response. The key takeaway is that KAPE can speed up Windows forensic triage by using predefined targets and modules to collect relevant artifacts and run analysis tools efficiently.

  • The article is titled “KAPE 101: A Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor Cheatsheet.”
  • The article is about KAPE, which the title identifies as the Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor.
  • The article presents itself as an introductory “101” resource for KAPE.
  • The article is framed as a cheatsheet for KAPE.

5 reasons to bring application security data into your exposure management platform — Optional

Integrating application security scanner data into an exposure management platform helps security teams connect code flaws to real-world business risk, prioritize the most dangerous vulnerabilities, and coordinate remediation across development and security teams. Tenable argues this is especially important as AI coding tools increase the volume of vulnerable code and scanner findings.

  • The article argues that application security data often remains isolated in code-scanning tools, making it difficult to correlate code flaws with security issues in cloud workloads, on-premises assets, operational technology systems, identity platforms, and other parts of the environment.
  • The article says AI coding tools are increasing application security challenges because developers using AI assistants commit code faster and introduce more security findings, while a cited source says 45% of AI-generated code contains known security flaws.
  • Integrating application security scanner data into an exposure management platform can give security teams code-to-runtime visibility, including where code is written and deployed, who owns it, where it runs, and its potential blast radius.
  • The article states that exposure management can help prioritize code vulnerabilities by considering factors such as whether assets are in production, user identities and entitlements, external accessibility, business criticality, application importance, and compliance requirements.
  • The article says Tenable One can ingest, analyze, and normalize static-code security data from application security tools, including Snyk data through a native connector and other tools through the Tenable One Open Connector.

New Webinar: Closing the Approval Gap in AI-Era Ad Tech — Optional

Reflectiz and Taboola’s on-demand webinar focuses on the “Approval Gap,” where approved marketing tags can load unvetted fourth-party scripts that access sensitive browser-side data. The key takeaway is that security teams need continuous visibility and monitoring of ad tech scripts, not one-time vendor approval, especially as AI accelerates changes in the web supply chain.

  • The article describes the “Approval Gap” as the difference between the marketing vendor code a security team approved and the third- and fourth-party scripts actually running in users’ browsers.
  • Reflectiz co-founder and CEO Idan Cohen and Taboola Director of Product Omri Ariav discuss the issue from both the security-monitoring and ad tech platform perspectives in an on-demand webinar.
  • The article says fourth-party scripts loaded by approved marketing tags can access forms, checkout fields, and customer data because they run client-side in the browser.
  • The article states that AI-driven ad tech is creating new integrations, endpoints, and data flows quickly, making one-time approvals outdated.
  • The webinar promises a three-step playbook to inventory, monitor, and govern the web supply chain without creating operational friction.

Firefox, Chrome, Adobe, and VMware Updates Fix Multiple Critical Security Flaws — Optional

Mozilla, Google, Adobe, and Broadcom released patches for multiple critical vulnerabilities affecting Firefox, Chrome, Adobe products, and VMware Avi Load Balancer. Organizations should update quickly, especially because public exploit code exists for two Firefox flaws even though no active exploitation has been reported.

  • Mozilla released Firefox 152.0.6 to fix two critical flaws, CVE-2026-15718 and CVE-2026-15719, and said public exploit code exists but no attacks in the wild are known.
  • Google shipped fixes for 15 Chrome security flaws, including two critical use-after-free bugs in Ozone, CVE-2026-15764 and CVE-2026-15765.
  • Adobe published security updates for 88 vulnerabilities, including critical flaws in ColdFusion, Commerce, Experience Manager, and Illustrator.
  • Adobe fixed eight ColdFusion vulnerabilities in ColdFusion 2025 Update 11 and ColdFusion 2023 Update 22, several of which could lead to arbitrary code execution.
  • Broadcom released a fix for CVE-2026-47865, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware Avi Load Balancer that could allow network access to the Avi Control plane.

A Trivia Game at Black Hat Asia & the Case for Network Visibility | Corelight — Optional

Corelight used a trivia game at Black Hat Asia to highlight how strong network visibility helps security teams detect threats, investigate faster, and make better decisions. The main takeaway is that seeing what is happening across the network remains foundational to effective cybersecurity.

  • The article is from Corelight and is titled “A Trivia Game at Black Hat Asia & the Case for Network Visibility.”
  • The article discusses a trivia game at Black Hat Asia.
  • The article connects the trivia game to an argument for network visibility.

SASE Has An AI Blind Spot. Inspecting Packets Is No Longer Enough. — Optional

Traditional SASE inspection is losing visibility as encrypted protocols, browser-based workflows, and AI agents move sensitive data interactions beyond the network layer. The article argues enforcement must shift to the browser and endpoint so organizations can inspect user intent and data before it leaves the device.

  • The article argues that traditional SASE architectures based on routing traffic through cloud proxies are struggling because enterprise work now happens across SaaS applications, browsers, generative AI tools, browser extensions, and autonomous agents.
  • Modern protocols such as TLS 1.3, HTTP/3, and certificate pinning can block proxy-based decryption and inspection, forcing organizations to create bypass exceptions that reduce security coverage.
  • The article says AI and agentic workflows expose a visibility gap because a network proxy may only see an encrypted HTTPS connection and not the intent or content of actions such as pulling proprietary code or internal documentation.
  • The article claims that routing sessions through distant cloud inspection paths can add latency and degrade user experience, which may encourage users to seek shadow workarounds.
  • The article proposes enforcing policy at the browser and endpoint so copy, paste, and prompt content can be inspected locally before data leaves the device, while trusted traffic can take a direct path to its destination.
